entry.title: How SAP Business AI looks like in Cloud ERP
entry.content:
As a Customer Success Manager at SAP for Cloud ERP, I have a front-row seat to something that keeps surprising me: the moment customers realize that AI is not a feature to switch on but a transformation to lean into.

It started at our Customer Success Day for Cloud ERP, where I presented SAP Business AI sessions (since 2024) covering the announcement of SAP Business AI and its first wave of scenarios. The energy in the room told me this conversation was far from over. So here I am, continuing it.

In this post, I want to walk you through three things:

  1. AI use cases embedded within real business processes
  2. What SAP Business AI offers
  3. SAP's direction on AI Agents — and why it matters now

 

SAP's AI Vision: The Three Pillars That Make It Real

You have probably heard this from analysts, consultants, and technology leaders alike: AI is only as good as the data and processes it runs on. SAP has built its entire AI strategy around that truth, and anchored it in three interdependent pillars.

  • Applications — SAP's end-to-end business suite connects every corner of an organization. Every transaction — in finance, procurement, logistics, or HR — originates from a single integrated framework. Processes like order-to-cash or procure-to-pay are not just digitized; they are AI-ready by design.
  • Unmatched Data — Through SAP Business Data Cloud, information from both SAP and non-SAP sources is harmonized into a unified layer. AI agents receive a 360-degree view of the business, and no time wasted reconciling conflicting definitions, no gaps in context. Data is instantly understood in its business meaning.
  • Unrivaled AI — Bring the right data to specialized agents orchestrated by Joule, and you unlock continuous optimization across every line of business. This is not isolated automation — it is an interconnected system that learns, adapts, and scales.

These three pillars create a self-reinforcing cycle of innovation. Applications feed clean processes. Clean processes feed trusted data. Trusted data powers AI. And AI, in turn, continuously improves the applications. That is the engine behind the SAP Business Suite.

We Are Already Living With AI — Are We Getting the Most From It?

Think about your own workday. You rely on AI to suggest the right words in an email. To generate a meeting summary. To autocomplete a search query. To recommend how to handle a support ticket. We have come to depend on AI assistance as a natural part of our workflow, and that is not a criticism. It is a signal.

But here is the honest reality: most of us are enabling one feature here, one capability there. And isolated AI features do not deliver the step-change efficiency that businesses need. The real value emerges when AI is embedded in an end-to-end process, not just at individual touchpoints.

What End-to-End AI Looks Like in Practice

To make this concrete, consider how an AI-enabled workflow responds to a critical business disruption, from detection all the way through to resolution. Here is an example scenario that SAP Situation Handling, combined with Joule, is designed to support:

  1.   Detect — Critical business issues are identified automatically, without waiting for a human to notice.
  2.   Alert — Relevant users are notified through SAP Fiori Launchpad, email, or SAP Mobile Start — the right person, at the right moment, in the right channel.
  3.   Navigate — Using Joule, users can surface related issues on demand, access additional context, and navigate directly to the impacted application.
  4.   Contextualize — Relevant business data is presented to support a fully informed decision.
  5.   Resolve — Generative AI provides tailored resolution recommendations, grounded in the actual business context — not generic suggestions.

No siloed dashboards. No manual correlation. No guesswork. This is what AI-assisted, process-integrated intelligence looks like in practice.

 

The Four Building Blocks of SAP Business AI

When my customer asks me:  What are the AI features/scenarios that I can activate now? 

Here is my answer to them:  What would you like to achieve with AI?

Let me break it down why. To understand where AI is embedded across SAP's Cloud ERP portfolio, it helps to think in lego building blocks(archetypes).  Each represents a distinct way AI adds value, and together they provide a consistent, scalable model for embedding intelligence across domains: finance, sales, procurement, logistics, manufacturing, and beyond.

  • AI for User Experience — AI embedded directly in Cloud ERP applications, generating text, producing summaries, or writing code, helping users work faster and with greater confidence. 
  • AI for Engagement — Conversational AI like Joule, embedded in the flow of work. Joule handles complex, multi-turn interactions that previously required significant human effort to resolve.
  • AI for Automation — Repetitive, rule-bound tasks — document classification, invoice matching, data processing — handled automatically, freeing teams for higher-value work.
  • AI for Insight and Decision-Making — Predictive capabilities such as demand forecasting, late payment prediction, and risk identification — paired with intelligent recommendations and next-best actions — helping organizations move from reactive to proactive.

 

 

The Next Chapter: From Joule Assistant to Joule Work/ Agent / Studio

A year ago, the conversation was about Joule as an AI assistant > a powerful copilot embedded across SAP applications. Today, that conversation has grown considerably.

The reasoning capability of AI foundation models has advanced at a pace few anticipated. Models can now work through complex, multi-step problems with human-like judgment. That capability is the foundation for AI agents : systems that do not just respond, but act. And in the enterprise, that distinction matters enormously.

SAP's strategy for AI agents is built around two commitments:

  • Best-in-class agents on standard business processes — Purpose-built, enterprise-ready agents deeply integrated with SAP's core business workflows — so customers benefit immediately without custom development.
  • An open framework for custom agents — The Joule Framework enables customers and partners to build their own agents, leveraging the same infrastructure SAP uses internally. Enterprise-grade capability, democratized.

The goal is not to replace human judgment. It is to put the right intelligence in the right place, at the right moment so that the people who run these businesses can focus on the decisions that truly require them.

Closing Thoughts

SAP Business AI is an architectural shift in how enterprise software works. AI is no longer bolted on after the fact. It is woven into the fabric of every process, every transaction, every interaction. With the latest announcement of "Autonomous Enterprise" at SAPPHIRE 2026, SAP is ready to help businesses transform how they operate.

The organizations that gain the most will not be those that activate the most features. They will be the ones who think end-to-end "with the business outcome in mind" and let AI do the same.

entry.title: Customize Your Emails for Situation Handling in the Extended Framework
entry.content:
Situation Handling

Situation Handling in SAP S/4HANA Cloud alerts users about issues requiring their attention. You can use SAP-delivered templates or create your own use cases to detect critical business issues.

With the extended framework for Situation Handling in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2608, you can customize the emails for object-based situations. This blog post explains the default notification settings and the customizing option.

Alert the right users about situations

Situation Handling uses multiple channels to inform the users about critical business situations that require their attention. This includes:

  • Situation descriptions embedded in business apps
  • Notification channels in SAP Fiori launchpad and emails

Situation Handling is designed to keep users well informed and support them in their daily work.

Situation Handling emails

One way of informing users about critical business situations is by email. Emails are triggered together with notifications and sent automatically when situations occur, provided the notification option is activated.

Activate emails together with notifications

Let’s look at the standard notification settings of a situation type and their impact on emails:

  • Notify all after creation / Processor only after update: An email is sent to all recipients when a situation has occurred and to the processor when a situation was updated
  • No notification after closing: No email is sent to anybody
  • Notify all after reopening: An email is sent to all recipients

You can also define custom notification settings and their related impact. Whenever a notification is sent, an email is sent as well.

Email templates are predefined

Situation emails use predefined templates that are automatically assigned to the situation type. This means no additional configuration is required.

The predefined email template consists of the email subject and the email body. Most parts of the email body are fixed and cannot be changed. This contains the greeting, the links to SAP Fiori launchpad and to detailed situation information as well as the source and the sign-off. The customizable email text is the one that describes the situation.

Adapt email subject and email text

You have two options to adapt the email template.

  • Reuse the notification title as email subject and the notification text in the email body.
  • Add a specific plain text to the email body and go with an SAP-defined email subject.

The situation type automatically inherits the setting of the situation template. You can change the settings in the situation type at any time. Afterwards, the new emails are generated according to the updated configuration.

If you change a situation template later, it has no effect on existing situation types.

Reuse notification title and text in email subject and body

You can reuse the notification title as the email subject, including variables such as plant, supplier, or contract ID. The reuse option also inserts the notification text into the email body, where variables can be used as well. The email preview shows how the email will look like.

Additionally, you can select if notifications are aggregated or not.

  • No Aggregation: Send a notification and email for every situation instance.
  • Aggregate by Field: Group notifications as well as emails by a selected field, for instance, supplier.
  • Aggregate All: Group all notifications as well as all emails.

Let’s check how the different settings affect the emails.

Non-aggregated notifications and emails

If you choose non-aggregated notifications, a separate notification and an email are sent for each situation. Initially, notification title and text are already copied from the situation title and text. Title and text can be also reused as the email subject and in the email body. This provides an efficient configuration experience.

The email template contains links to both, the SAP Fiori launchpad and the specific situation.

Reuse option: non-aggregated email

Aggregated notifications and emails

Reuse works the same way for aggregated notifications. Whether you aggregate all notifications or aggregate them by field, the title and text are copied to the email template’s subject and body.

For a meaningful representation, you can use only character-based variables such as strings. In addition, the count variable indicates how many situations are aggregated. If you select Aggregate by Field, you can use the aggregated by variable to show the field used for aggregation.

Because of the aggregation, the email template no longer includes a link to a specific situation; instead, it shows the generic link to SAP Fiori launchpad.

Reuse option: aggregated email by field

Aggregation by field allows more specific end user texts by including this field as variable.

If you aggregate all notifications and emails, the texts will be more generic.

Reuse option: aggregated email for all situations

Note: Be aware of the variables you are using in the email. They may contain personal data. Review the variables to prevent unintended exposure in emails. Also make sure that the data is managed in accordance with the legal requirements and business needs.

Specific email text with SAP-defined email subject

Alternatively, you can add plain texts without variables in the email body and use a default subject defined by SAP. This option makes sure that the email does not include business-sensitive data or personal data which may conflict with legal requirements or business needs.

You also get a preview of the email with this option. Let’s take a look at how this works in detail.

Non-aggregated notifications and emails

For non-aggregated notifications, an email is sent for each situation using the default subject and the embedded custom email text.

The email template includes links to both the SAP Fiori launchpad and the specific situation.

Custom option: non-aggregated email

Aggregated notifications and emails

Aggregated emails also have a default subject and a custom email text without variables.

Because the emails are aggregated, you no longer see the link to a specific situation in the email template but the generic link to SAP Fiori launchpad.

Custom option: aggregated email by field

Since the custom email texts do not contain variables, they remain generic for both aggregation options.

Custom option: aggregated email for all situations

Now you are all set and know how you can configure emails matching your business needs.

Further Information

You find more blog posts in the Best Practices section of Intelligent Situation Handling in the SAP Community. And you can visit SAP Help Portal for further guidance on Situation Handling.

entry.title: Situation Handling in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition: Your Quick Start Guide to Proactive
entry.content:
What is Situation Handling?

Situation Handling framework is part of SAP S/4HANA Cloud that automatically detects, tracks, and informs about issues in your business that require the attention of specified users. You can choose from various options to inform your users about such situations in your business such as notifications, list views, or dedicated object pages. Also, you can provide your users with data related to these situations for informed decisions, and proposed actions to solve the situations as quickly and efficiently as possible. 

You can define your own use cases by choosing from a wide range of standard situation templates from various business areas, complete with text proposals by which end users are informed about the situations. You can adapt them easily to fit your requirements. 

Situation Handling allows you to track and collect comprehensive analytical data on business situations and how they are handled, which helps you monitor and continuously improve your own business processes as part of an Intelligent ERP.

Why Situation Handling Matters — The Business Case

In most organizations, business exceptions are discovered too late. A billing document doesn’t post. A purchase contract quietly expires. A stock transport order slips past its deadline. By the time someone notices, the damage — missed SLAs, revenue leakage, escalations and financial losses — is already done.

Situation Handling flips this reactive model on its head. It proactively detects issues in real time, alerts the right owner, and guides them to resolution before business impact occurs.

Here’s the shift at a glance:

❌ Without Situation Handling✔️With Situation Handling
Issues discovered too lateProactive real-time detection
Manual monitoring & chasingAutomated alerts with clear ownership
Missed deadlines & SLA breachesProvide contextual information to support informed decision-making​
Revenue leakageFaster billing & improved cash flow
Reactive firefighting cultureProactive intelligent operations culture
High cost of exception management

Reduced manual effort & overhead

Two Powerful Framework Layers

Situation Handling is delivered in two complementary layers, so you can start simple and scale as your needs grow.

FrameworkDescriptionEffort
Standard Framework100+ SAP-delivered, ready-to-activate Situation Templates across Finance, Sales, Procurement, Supply Chain, and ManufacturingMinimal — configuration only
Extended Framework20+ SAP-delivered templates, plus the ability to build fully custom situations using objects from your system, such as CDS views or business eventsHigher flexibility, more implementation effort

Best-Practice Framework: Selecting High-Value Templates

Don’t boil the ocean. Start smart. Deliver value fast.

With 100+ templates available, the temptation is to review them all. Resist it. Follow this three-step approach instead.

Step 1 — Align with Business Pain Points First

Start with your top KPIs and known pain points rather than the full template catalog. Typical high-impact starting points include:

  • Finance → Billing Documents Not Posted to Accounting
  • Procurement → Expiring Purchase Contracts / Low Quotations Received
  • Sales → Sales Orders Blocked for Delivery / Quotation Close to Expiry
  • Supply Chain → Stock Transport Orders Overdue / Physical Inventory Deviations

Step 2 — Map to SAP Pre-Delivered Templates

Once pain points are identified, consult the Situation Handling Use Case Catalog on the SAP Help Portal. Templates can be filtered by Line of Business:

Line of BusinessExample Pre-Delivered Templates
Finance
  • Requested Payment Timeout Issue
  • Requested Payment Status Issue
  • Event-Based Product Costing Errors
  • Change of Credit Limit
  • Monitor General Business-Critical Errors in Application Jobs for Convergent Invoicing

and many more templates.

Sourcing & Procurement
  • Expiration of Purchase Contracts
  • Approaching Delivery Date of Centrally Managed Purchase Requisitions
  • Overdue Items Of Replicated Purchase Order
  • Overdue Centrally Managed PO Items
  • Quantity Deficit in Supplier's Delivery

and many more templates.

Sales
  • Billing Documents Not Posted
  • Service Order Not Scheduled
  • Solution Order Delivery Date Changed
  • Project Execution Dates Changed
  • Project Net Value Changed

and many more templates.

Service
  • Service Maint. Plan Mass Schedule Issue
  • Repair Confirmations Required
  • Processing of In-House Repair Overdue
  • Executing Service Employee Missing
  • Billing for Service Order Not Completed
  • Service Contract Item Not Released

and many more templates.

Note: 

  • These are just sample SAP -Predelivered templates, more details on pre-delivered templates, can be found in here: Use Case.
  • Both the Standard and Extended frameworks come with pre-delivered templates. The Extended Framework additionally allows building fully custom scenarios — ideal when no standard template covers your use case.

 

Step 3 — Evaluate Feasibility & Business Impact

For each shortlisted template, score it across three dimensions:

DimensionEvaluation Question
FrequencyHow often does this situation occur in the business? (Daily / Weekly / Monthly)
Financial ImpactWhat is the cost, risk, or revenue exposure if this goes unaddressed?
Implementation EffortStandard = minimal config, fast go-live · Extended = more effort, higher flexibility

 

Scoring Tip:For your first wave of quick wins, prioritize templates that score HIGH on Frequency + Financial Impact and LOW on Implementation Effort.

 AI + Joule Integration: Next-Gen Intelligent Operations

Situation Handling is now Joule-powered — bringing conversational AI directly into your exception management workflow.

  • Joule (SAP’s AI Copilot) surfaces situations on demand through natural language conversation.
  • Users simply ask: "Show me my situations?" — and Joule responds instantly.
  • Joule guides users directly to the right Fiori app.
  • The result: proactive detection + AI-driven conversation = true intelligent operations.

Video: Situation Handling in SAP S/4HANA Cloud featuring Joule

Extensibility: Build Your Own Custom Use Cases

No standard template for your scenario? Build one — no core modifications ever needed.

Here’s the custom use case creation path using the Extended Framework:

  1. Model your Situation Object → Business Object / CDS View

entry.title: Notification Trigger Based on GRN Against a PO
entry.content:
Introduction

Timely visibility of Goods Receipt Notes (GRNs) is essential for procurement teams to monitor purchase order fulfillment, track material receipts, and ensure smooth supplier coordination. While SAP S/4HANA Cloud provides Situation Handling capabilities, configuring a notification based on Material Document posting can be challenging due to semantic key limitations in the standard setup.

In this blog, we will explore how to configure a custom Situation Handling solution in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition to automatically notify the Procurement Team whenever a GRN is posted against a Purchase Order (PO). The solution leverages a custom CDS view, custom Situation Object, Situation Scenario, and Situation Type to provide real-time notifications through the SAP Fiori Launchpad.

Business Requirement

The Procurement team should receive a notification whenever a GRN is posted against a Purchase Order.

The notification should:

  • Be triggered automatically after GR posting.
  • Be visible in SAP Fiori Launchpad.
  • Allow users to navigate directly to the relevant business object.
  • Exclude GRNs created for Production Orders.

Challenge with Standard CDS View

Initially, I attempted to use the standard CDS view I_MaterialDocumentItem_2 directly in the Situation Object configuration.

The semantic key was maintained using the MaterialDocument field.

However, the Situation Object activation failed with a data loss error.

 

Root Cause Analysis

The standard Material Document event uses:

  • MaterialDocument
  • MaterialDocumentPostingYear

as the business object key.

Since MaterialDocument supports only 10 characters and the event payload contains both document number and posting year, the combined key length exceeds the permitted size, resulting in a data loss error during configuration.

1. Create a Custom CDS View

To overcome above stated limitation, a custom CDS view must be created that concatenates the Material Document Number and Material Document Posting Year into a single calculated field, which can then be used as the semantic object key in the Situation Object configuration.

To create the CDS view:

  • First open the Custom CDS View app and click on create. 
  • Use the SAP standard CDS view I_MaterialDocumentItem_2 as the data source.
  • Navigate to the Elements tab.
  • Create a Calculated Field that concatenates the Material Document Number and Material Document Posting Year.
  • Add the newly created calculated field to the CDS view output.

Publish the CDS view.

The calculated field serves as a unique key and helps overcome the standard field length limitation encountered when configuring the Situation Object.

This is the calculation field logic - CONCAT( MaterialDocumentYear, MaterialDocument )

 



2. To meet the above requirement, we need to create a custom Situation Type to trigger notifications whenever a GRN is posted against a PO. This configuration involves the following three SAP Fiori apps:

2a. Manage Situation Objects
2b. Manage Situation Scenarios
2c. Manage Situation Types – Extended

2a. Manage Situation Object

In the General Information section, enter the required details such as the Situation Object Name and Description.

 


In the Structure section, maintain the details as shown below. For the Structure Name, select the custom CDS view that was created in the previous step.

 


Next, configure the Event tab by using the standard Material Document Posting event.

Event Details:

  • Event Category: ABAP Class
  • Event Object: CL_MMIM_MATDOC_EVENT


Configure the Navigation Target to enable users to navigate directly from the notification to the relevant SAP Fiori application.

Note: The Semantic Object (MATERIALDOCUMENT_NO) Key should be mapped to the calculated field created in the custom CDS view. If the standard Material Document field is used, the system may throw a data loss error due to the standard character length limitation.


 


Configure the required End User Actions so that end users can view the notification and navigate directly to the relevant application from the SAP Fiori Launchpad.


 

2b. Manage Situation Scenarios

Navigate to the Manage Situation Scenarios app and choose Create to define a new Situation Scenario. Enter the required details in the respective sections as shown below.


In the General Information section, enter the required details such as the Situation Scenario Name, Description, and other relevant information as shown below.

 


Next, specify the Anchor Object, which is used to identify the business object that triggers the situation and provides the relevant event information.

Ensure that the Semantic Key is mapped to the calculated field created in the custom CDS view. The semantic key defined in the Situation Scenario must match the CDS view's calculated field to ensure that the event data is processed correctly.

In the Instance Key section, maintain the newly created calculated field along with the Purchase Order Number to uniquely identify each situation instance.

Alternatively, you can use only the newly created calculated field if it sufficiently meets the business requirement.


Configure the General Actions section to allow users to access and view the situation directly from the SAP Fiori Launchpad.


Finally, configure the Situation Trigger by maintaining the required details as shown below. This configuration determines when the situation should be created and the notification should be triggered.

2c. Manage Situation Types – Extended

In this step, create a Situation Template and a Situation Type, and then activate the Situation Type to enable notifications whenever a Goods Receipt Note (GRN) is posted against a Purchase Order (PO).

 


In the Manage Situation Types – Extended app, click Create Situation Template.

Enter the required details, including the Situation Template Name, and select the Situation Scenario that was created in the previous step.

 

 

After selecting the Situation Scenario, maintain all the configurations defined in the previous steps, including the Situation Object, Event Configuration, and End User Actions, within the Situation Template.


 

 

 


In this example, the filter condition is defined such that the Purchase Order Number must not be empty. This excludes GRNs posted against Production Orders and ensures that only GRNs related to Purchase Orders are visible to the Procurement Team and other relevant users.

 

 


To distribute notifications to the Procurement Team, create and assign a team under the PROC Team category.

 

Create and Activate the Situation Type

Once the Situation Template has been created, an option to Create Situation Type will be available on the same page.

Click Create Situation Type, maintain the required settings, and activate it.

After activation, whenever a GRN is posted against a Purchase Order, the system automatically generates a situation and sends a notification to the designated recipients.

Notification Output

The notification will appear in the SAP Fiori Launchpad as shown below.

 

Conclusion

In this blog, we demonstrated how to configure a custom Situation Handling solution to automatically notify the Procurement Team whenever a Goods Receipt Note (GRN) is posted against a Purchase Order. By creating a custom CDS view and leveraging the standard Situation Handling framework, we were able to successfully trigger notifications based on Material Document posting events.

This approach provides real-time visibility of PO-based goods receipts, improves collaboration between procurement and warehouse teams, and reduces the need for manual monitoring. It also showcases how SAP S/4HANA Cloud extensibility can be used to address specific business requirements while continuing to leverage standard SAP capabilities.

entry.title: Manyat Thinking: Not Every Problem Needs a Notification — Designing Business Attention in SAP
entry.content:
Manyat Thinking: Not Every Problem Needs a Notification — Designing Business Attention in SAP S/4HANA

Business First. SAP Second.

Introduction

In SAP, we can detect many things.

  • A Goods Receipt can create an event.
  • A warehouse process can generate an exception.
  • Transportation tracking can identify a delay.
  • A customer requirement can become at risk.
  • A process can detect an unexpected change.

But one question should come before designing another notification:

Does this problem actually require human attention?

Because detecting a problem and notifying a person are two different decisions.

I started thinking about this from a simple Goods Receipt scenario, but the same logic can be applied across EWM, TM/GTT, SD, MM, Procurement and other business processes.

1. It Started With a Simple GR Scenario

Imagine a Purchase Order for 100 units. The warehouse receives only 60 units.

The first reaction could be:

But should Procurement immediately receive a notification? Not necessarily.

Suppose the supplier has already confirmed: "The remaining 40 units will arrive tomorrow." And the customer also needs the material tomorrow. There is a quantity difference, but there may be no immediate business exception:

The transaction did not change. The business context changed. That is where notification design becomes interesting.

2. Event Is Not an Exception

A system event simply tells us: something happened. But the business needs to know: does this matter?

Therefore:

Event ≠ Business Exception

But even when a business exception exists, another question remains: does someone actually need to act? This gives us a broader decision logic:

 

Exception ≠ Notification

3. The First Filter: Can the Existing Process Handle It?

This became one of the strongest checks during my analysis.

Suppose TM detects a transportation problem. Before creating another notification, I would first ask:

Is the existing TM/GTT visibility and transportation process already providing the required handling?

For example, GTT/TM may already provide transportation visibility such as vehicle tracking, location, ETA, transportation events, and shipment visibility.

If the responsible transportation process can already manage the situation through its existing capabilities, then creating another notification simply because a problem was detected may add no value.

If the responsible process already provides the required visibility and handling, don't create another notification just because an exception exists.

Manyat Principle:

Let the responsible process handle what it is already designed to handle.

4. GTT: Visibility Is Not Automatically Notification

Transportation makes this distinction very clear.

Suppose Customer Commitment = 6:00 PM, Current ETA = 5:30 PM. GTT is already tracking the truck, and TM already has the transportation visibility.

Why should someone receive "Truck ETA is 5:30 PM" when that information is already available? Think about the difference:

Visibility ≠ Notification

Even if traffic data predicts that the ETA could move beyond the customer deadline, that is initially a risk signal — it does not automatically mean a business exception has occurred.

If later the carrier confirms a breakdown and the ETA becomes 7:15 PM, the business situation has materially changed. The question should therefore not simply be "Did GTT detect something?" The better question is "Does someone now need to take action?"

5. What About Changing the Truck?

Suppose Truck A becomes unavailable and TM assigns Truck B:

Should SD receive a notification? No. Changing the truck is part of TM's transportation responsibility — TM handles it. EWM may receive the updated transportation information through the normal process or integration if it needs that information for execution.

But turning every normal transportation change into a notification creates unnecessary noise.

Principle:

Normal process handling should remain normal process handling. A change by itself does not automatically justify a notification.

6. Detection Does Not Decide the Recipient

Now consider a warehouse availability issue. EWM identifies: Alternate Warehouse Stock = 5 EA, Reserved Stock = 3 EA, Actually Free = 2 EA.

EWM has detected the availability conflict. But the real business question may be: how will we fulfil the customer's commitment? That decision may belong to SD. SD may coordinate with MM/Procurement for additional supply, and EWM may execute the resulting warehouse activity later.

Detection ≠ Ownership

The process that detects the exception is not necessarily the process that should receive the notification.

7. Notification Recipient and Resolution Team Can Be Different

The person receiving the notification does not necessarily have to be the only person involved in solving the problem.

SD may coordinate with MM/Procurement for supply, TM for transportation, and EWM for warehouse execution.

The notification recipient and the people involved in resolution do not have to be the same.

The notification should reach the person who needs to make or initiate the next meaningful business decision or action.

8. EWM Exception Handling: Not Every Exception Needs Another Alert

EWM already provides exception-handling capabilities for warehouse execution. Warehouse tasks can encounter operational deviations, and EWM can react to those exceptions according to the configured process.

Suppose there is no customer impact, no escalation, no business decision, no manual intervention — then why create another notification? The exception may still be useful as operational, audit or analytical information where appropriate.

Important distinction:

Exception data does not automatically mean exception notification.

9. POSC Shows Another Side of the Same Thinking

The same principle can be seen with Process-Oriented Storage Control (POSC):

If the business requires mandatory process steps or control points, POSC can help control the expected warehouse process. But should every POSC step generate a notification? No — because POSC and notification solve different problems.

Process control manages execution. Notification manages attention.

If POSC is already controlling the required warehouse sequence, creating notifications for every normal process step would simply turn process execution into noise.

10. What If the Problem Solves Itself?

Consider: EWM detects an allocation issue, the system automatically corrects it, no customer impact, no manual intervention, no business decision.

Should somebody receive a notification? Not necessarily. The event or exception may still be retained for analysis, audit or trend monitoring where appropriate, but disturbing a person is unnecessary if there is no action to take.

Manyat Principle:

A self-resolved exception may need a record, but it does not necessarily need a notification.

11. Risk Is Not Automatically an Exception

Consider: Customer Requirement = 6:00 PM, Current ETA = 5:30 PM, Predicted ETA = 6:20 PM.

Should we immediately notify someone? Not necessarily — this is a risk signal, and the commitment has not necessarily been breached. Later:

Now the situation is materially different.

Risk Signal ≠ Business Exception

A monitoring system can continuously observe risk without continuously interrupting people.

12. Physical Reality Matters

Consider: Customer Order = 100, Goods Received = 100, Picking Complete, Packing Complete, Goods Physically Ready in Staging. Then the customer cancels the order.

The document changes. But does the physical warehouse movement disappear? No — the goods are still physically in the warehouse.

Document Cancellation ≠ Physical Movement Reversal

This is important in warehouse architecture because business documents and physical execution do not always change at exactly the same moment. Before designing a notification, understand the physical reality as well as the system state.

13. Existing Capability Before New Design

This became one of my strongest checks against overengineering.

Suppose an unplanned warehouse or yard requirement appears. Before creating a new notification mechanism, ask:

Does SAP already provide a capability for this scenario?

For example, an unplanned yard or warehouse movement may be handled through existing Ad-Hoc capabilities, depending on the specific process and configuration.

Manyat Principle:

Before designing something new, check what already exists.

14. The Notification Decision Framework

After going through these scenarios, I would use the following sequence:

The last option is important. Sometimes the correct design is nothing.

15. Where Does Situation Handling Fit?

SAP Situation Handling provides useful building blocks for this type of design. Depending on the specific SAP product, release and situation type, it can work with concepts such as conditions, situation instances, recipient determination, teams and responsibilities, notification settings, monitoring, and notification aggregation.

This means the technical capability can support a separation between business conditions and the eventual notification strategy. Instead of:

the thinking can become:

The exact capabilities and available fields depend on the specific SAP product, release and situation type, so the technical implementation still needs validation.

16. Notification Aggregation

There is another useful capability when notification volume genuinely becomes a problem.

Suppose Procurement has 3 Quantity Exceptions, 2 Supplier Confirmation Issues, and 5 Other Relevant Situations. Sending ten separate notifications may create unnecessary noise.

But aggregation should be an optimization, not the first answer to every notification problem:

 

Grouping should reduce noise, not reduce responsiveness.

17. The Architecture I Would Start With

Rather than beginning with "Which notification do we configure?" I would start with:

Only after this should we ask about the SAP technical implementation.

18. The Real Goal

The goal of a notification system should not be Maximum Notifications. It should be Maximum Relevance.

 

These situations are different. But they all lead to the same question:

Does somebody actually need to do something?

19. My Final Manyat Principle

After looking at these scenarios, I would summarize the thinking like this:

 

A problem is not automatically a notification.

First understand the problem. Then understand the business impact. Then check whether the responsible process can already handle it. Then identify who owns the next meaningful action. Only then decide whether human attention is required. And only after that should we design the notification mechanism.

Conclusion

The objective should not be to make SAP notify people about everything. The objective should be to make SAP provide the right information, to the right process, at the right time, with the right level of human attention.

Sometimes that solution will be Notification. Sometimes Monitoring. Sometimes Tracking. Sometimes Standard exception handling. Sometimes Aggregation. And sometimes — Nothing.

Because doing nothing can also be a valid design decision when the existing process already handles the situation and no human intervention is required.

Don't start by designing the notification. Start by designing the business response.

If another business problem appears, don't simply add another notification. Understand the problem. Check the existing capability. Identify the owner. Decide whether human attention is actually required. Then design the simplest solution that solves the business need.

Manyat Thinking

Business First. SAP Second.

"The best automation is not the one that tells humans about everything. It is the one that knows when humans actually need to know."

Rahul Kumar | Manyat Thinking

SAP EWM | SAP TM | Warehouse & Supply Chain Process Thinking | Business-First Solution Design

entry.title: Notification Grouping Is Not About Fewer Alerts — It Is About Better Business Attention
entry.content:
Notification Grouping Is Not About Fewer Alerts

It Is About Better Business Attention

Business First. SAP Second.

Introduction

In SAP, notifications are designed to bring situations requiring user attention to the right people.

As business processes become increasingly connected across functions such as MM, SD, EWM, TM, and Yard, users may receive a growing number of notifications.

At first, the solution may appear simple:

"There are too many notifications. Let's group them."

But is reducing the number of notifications really the objective? Imagine a team receiving 20 notifications. If we group them into one notification, the number becomes one. Looks better. But what if one of those 20 situations requires action within the next 15 minutes, while the other 19 can wait until the end of the day?

We reduced the notification count. But did we improve the business? Not necessarily.

Should notification grouping be designed simply to reduce notification volume — or to improve business attention?

1. Start With the Business Situation

Before deciding whether messages should be grouped, first understand the business requirement: What is the business situation? Who needs to act? What attention is required? When is that attention required?

Only after understanding the business situation should we decide how the messages should be presented.

Grouping comes after understanding the requirement.

2. Same Business Context Can Be Grouped

Suppose several purchase orders have the same supplier-confirmation issue:

The individual items can still remain available for detailed processing. The important point is:

We are grouping the messages — not changing the underlying business responsibilities.

3. Grouping Does Not Mean Merging Business Responsibilities

Consider a business process involving multiple functions. These messages may be connected to the same overall business process. However, grouping them does not mean that EWM, MM, and SD become one responsibility.

Message grouping does not mean merging business responsibilities.

This distinction is fundamental.

4. Same Material Does Not Automatically Define the Group

A common technical attribute can support grouping, but it does not automatically define the business meaning. Several messages may refer to the same material, but that does not necessarily mean they represent the same business activity.

A common technical attribute can support grouping, but business context should determine whether the grouping is meaningful.

5. Grouping Does Not Mean Every Situation Needs a Notification

Another important distinction: Grouping ≠ Notification. A business may want information consolidated for operational visibility. That does not automatically mean every record requires a notification.

Grouping is about how information is presented or consolidated. Notification is about whether user attention is required.

6. Notification Overload Is a Business Problem

A high number of messages is not automatically a problem. The real problem begins when users spend significant time managing notifications instead of addressing the underlying business situations.

The trigger should therefore be "users are losing business attention because of notification volume" — not simply "the system generates many messages." This distinction changes the solution discussion.

7. Urgent Information Must Remain Visible

A grouping design should not make the urgent message difficult to identify. The objective is not simply to make ten messages look like one. The objective is to make the user's attention more effective.

Grouping should improve communication without hiding important information.

8. Grouping Can Exist Across Multiple Functions

A single business process can involve several functions. These activities can belong to the same overall business context. However, the responsibilities remain function-specific.

A common business context does not require a common recipient.

9. Group the Communication, Not the Responsibility

Grouping the messages should not change who performs the work. The EWM team remains responsible for EWM activities. The SD team remains responsible for SD activities.

The purpose of grouping is to improve how messages are communicated and managed — not to move work from one function to another.

Group the communication, not the responsibility.

10. Notification Timing Matters

Not every function needs a notification simply because it is part of the end-to-end process.

Notify when attention becomes necessary — not simply because an event occurred somewhere in the process.

11. A Technical Problem Can Have a Different Notification Path

Consider an EWM execution delay caused by a technical problem. The warehouse operation may still have enough time buffer to absorb the delay.

If the technical issue is resolved before it creates business impact, there may be no reason to notify every function involved in the overall process.

Notification should follow the required business attention, not simply the complete history of events.

12. Grouping Messages Does Not Merge Responsibilities

These messages may be managed within a common context. But the responsibilities remain separate:

The message may be grouped. The work is not.

13. Grouping Should Follow Business Context

The objects may be different. The vendor may be different. The customer may be different. But if the messages are meaningful to the user as one common business context, grouping may be useful.

This is why I would not start the design with "Which field should I group by?" I would start with "What common business context are these messages representing?" Only then should we determine the appropriate technical grouping approach.

14. If Standard Notification Already Works, Don't Redesign It

Suppose the standard notification process works correctly. The volume is acceptable. Users understand the messages. The responsible teams can act without difficulty. Then why introduce grouping? There may be no business reason.

Do not redesign a process merely because another design is technically possible.

If standard SAP already delivers the required business outcome, keep it. Grouping should be introduced because there is a genuine business need.

15. When Should We Consider Message Grouping?

Consider grouping when:

  • Many repetitive messages are generated.
  • Users experience notification overload.
  • Messages represent a useful common business context.
  • Individual messages add little additional communication value.
  • A consolidated presentation improves usability.
  • Important information remains visible.
  • Individual responsibilities remain unchanged.

Do not group simply because:

  • The records have the same material.
  • They happened at the same time.
  • They belong to the same customer or supplier.
  • The message count looks large.

16. Three Practical Cases

17. Compact Decision Matrix

A simple way to make the decision:

  • Standard process works, low volume → Keep individual notifications
  • Repetitive messages, high volume, same context → Consider grouping
  • High volume, different meanings → Keep separate
  • Common context, no action required → No notification needed
  • Mixed routine + urgent → Group carefully; keep urgent visible
  • Different functions, overall context common → Group communication only; keep responsibility separate

Group when it improves business attention — not merely when it reduces message count.

18. SAP Perspective

From an SAP perspective, Situation Handling provides mechanisms for identifying situations and bringing them to users' attention — situation types, templates, conditions and filters, responsibility determination, notification configuration and aggregation, aggregation by field, message-based thresholds, and resend options.

But the starting point remains the business requirement. The sequence I prefer is:

The technology supports the design. It should not define the business requirement.

19. Grouping Is a Communication Optimization

This is how I see notification architecture:

Grouping is therefore an optimization of how messages are communicated. It does not redefine who owns the business process, who performs the work, or which function is responsible. That responsibility remains intact.

20. The Real Goal

The goal is not Minimum Notifications. The goal is Maximum Relevant Business Attention.

If ten important messages need to remain visible individually, then ten notifications may be the right answer. If fifty repetitive messages create noise, grouping may be the better answer.

Does grouping help the user understand and manage the relevant business information more effectively?

If yes, consider it. If no, don't do it merely to reduce the number of notifications.

21. Manyat Thinking

Before configuring notification grouping, ask:

SAP Help References

SAP Help documentation confirms that Situation Handling is designed to identify business situations and bring them to the attention of the relevant users. It also provides configuration options for situation types, conditions, recipients, and notifications.

For notification grouping specifically, SAP documents the Aggregate Notifications capability. Depending on the situation type and configuration, notifications can be sent individually for each situation instance or as an aggregated notification. SAP also documents aggregation by a selected field for supported object-based situations.

This supports the principle discussed in this article: notification aggregation is a communication and attention-management option; it should be applied according to the business context rather than simply to reduce the number of notifications.

SAP Help Portal:

  • Situation Handling – SAP Help
  • Situation Display – SAP Help
  • Key Concepts in Situation Handling – SAP Help

Final Thought

A notification is not valuable because it exists. A grouped notification is not valuable simply because it contains many messages.

The real value comes from directing:

The right business attention → to the right person → at the right time.

And the most important distinction is:

We are grouping messages, not merging business responsibilities.

So I would summarize the Manyat principle as:

Don't configure SAP simply to produce fewer notifications. Configure it to deliver better business attention.

Manyat Thinking

Business First. SAP Second.

entry.title: Manyat Thinking: Weight Variance — Block the Risk, Not Every Truck
entry.content:
Manyat Thinking: Weight Variance — Block the Risk, Not Every Truck

A design perspective on tolerance-based discrepancy handling

across SAP EWM, TM, and Situation Handling

Business First. SAP Second.

Introduction

In warehouse and transportation operations, weight discrepancy is often treated as a simple control problem. The standard reaction can easily become:

Planned Weight ≠ Actual Weight → Block the Process

At first glance, this looks safe. But what happens when every discrepancy immediately stops the truck? The vehicle waits. The yard starts filling. Loading and dispatch operations slow down. And eventually, a control designed to protect the business can become an operational bottleneck.

Should every weight discrepancy block execution, or should the system first understand the level of risk?

A discrepancy should first be classified, not automatically blocked.

1.  The Ground Reality

Weight differences can appear at different points in the physical process: planned weight, loading weight, weighbridge weight, transportation execution data, receiving weight.

A difference can have several possible causes: scale calibration, moisture or natural weight loss, packaging differences, measurement variation, loading conditions, or an actual unexplained quantity difference.

So the system should not immediately treat every difference as the same type of exception.

What does this discrepancy actually mean for the business?

2.  The Traditional Approach

A simple control can look like this:

Technically, this looks controlled. Operationally, however, it can create another problem. If investigation takes time, the truck remains at the origin. Now imagine this happening across multiple vehicles:

The system has protected one control point but potentially damaged the overall warehouse flow.

So I would not start with "How can SAP block this truck?" I would start with:

What level of risk does this discrepancy represent?

3.  The Manyat Approach: Risk Classification

The architecture should introduce one additional decision layer.

This changes the architecture completely. The system is no longer saying Difference = Block. Instead:

Difference = Evaluate Risk

4.  But What If Blocking Costs More Than the Risk?

Suppose goods value is ₹5,000, but stopping the truck creates a delay penalty of ₹10,000:

"Control ka cost risk se bada to nahi ho gaya?"

In professional terms: is the cost of the control greater than the business risk we are trying to control? This does not mean cost should always override risk — a critical security or compliance risk may still require a hard block regardless of delay cost. The point is to make the decision consciously.

5.  Decision Flow

 The real control point is the decision.

6.  Three Business Decisions

Situation

7.  Example: +120 KG Difference

Plant A shipment: Planned Gross Weight = 10,000 KG, Tolerance = 50 KG, Actual Weight = 10,120 KG.

Tolerance breach does not automatically have to mean process block. It can mean: Evaluate the risk.

8.  Soft Attention Instead of Immediate Blocking

The truck does not automatically become the victim of the system's uncertainty.

9.  But If We Don't Block, How Do We Manage the Risk?

Continue ≠ Ignore. If a variance requires verification, the business still needs a control mechanism.

10.  Who Should Receive the Alert?

11.  Situation Handling: Attention, Not Enforcement

Situation Handling can bring the right business situation to the attention of the right person.

12.  Destination Verification

13.  Not Every Difference Means Theft

The business process should determine what the difference means.

14.  Soft Attention vs Hard Block

15.  Why This Architecture Is Different

16.  EWM, TM and Yard Should Not Be Designed in Isolation

17.  The Real Control Point Is Not the Truck

18.  Targeted Verification

19.  This Is Not "Ignore the Exception"

20.  SAP Configuration Comes After the Business Decision

21.  The Manyat Thinking Principle

Conclusion

A weight discrepancy is an important operational signal. But a signal should not automatically become a system lock.

What level of risk does this discrepancy represent, and what is the least disruptive control that still protects the business?

The architecture therefore becomes: Detect → Classify → Decide → Act → Validate Outcome.

Do not block every discrepancy. Block the risk that truly requires blocking.

MANYAT THINKING

Business First. SAP Second.

entry.title: Stop Overengineering Document Links Unlocking GOS as the Situation Handling Speed Layer
entry.content:
Stop Overengineering Document Links: Unlocking GOS as the Situation Handling Speed Layer

Manyat Thinking | Business First. SAP Second.

The Real Business Problem

A warehouse exception can look very simple on the ground. An operator may find a weight variance, a broken seal, a damaged pallet, or a product condition that requires visual evidence.

The natural reaction is often to start thinking about the SAP object, notification, document, repository, or integration that should be used.

But the better starting point is the business situation itself.

What does the business actually need at that moment?

Consider a simple broken-seal scenario. An operator receives a pallet and discovers that its seal is broken. The operator takes a photograph as evidence.

At this point, several different requirements exist.

The photograph is evidence. Someone needs to know that the exception requires attention. A physical action may follow, which is execution. Later, the business may need to understand what actually happened, which is history.

These requirements are connected, but they are not the same requirement.

That distinction is where the architecture should begin.

What Is Manyat Thinking?

Manyat Thinking is my personal business-first way of designing SAP solutions.

It starts with the physical situation, asks WHY, identifies the actual business requirement, and only then maps that requirement to the appropriate SAP capability and technical implementation.

The thinking flow is:

Ground Reality → Exception → WHY → Root Cause → Business Requirement → Business Decision → SAP Capability → Technical Implementation → Practical Application

This is not intended to replace standard SAP solution architecture or introduce a new SAP methodology.

It is simply a practical way of approaching an SAP problem from the business side first.

The core question is:

What does the business actually need, and which SAP capability naturally owns that requirement?

A Worked Example: Broken Seal

The operator has found a broken seal.

The first requirement is evidence. The photograph needs to remain associated with the relevant business context. Where supported by the relevant business object/application, GOS or the applicable attachment capability can provide that function.

The second requirement is attention. The photograph itself does not determine who needs to act. Situation Handling has a different responsibility: bringing the relevant business situation to the attention of the responsible user.

The third requirement is action. Suppose the responsible user decides that the affected HU must be moved to a clarification or quarantine area. The physical warehouse movement belongs to the existing EWM execution process.

The fourth requirement is history. After the warehouse action is completed, the business may need to know what happened, when it happened, and what warehouse execution was confirmed.

So the architecture becomes:

Evidence → GOS / Attachment Attention → Situation Handling Warehouse Action → EWM Execution Warehouse Execution History → EWM Warehouse Task History

This is the important architectural separation.

The problem is not really a single "notification/document" problem. It is several business requirements that happen to originate from the same physical exception.

One Business Situation, Different SAP Responsibilities

A common design mistake is to make one technical mechanism responsible for everything simply because all the information came from the same exception.

That is not necessary.

GOS / Attachment can maintain the supporting evidence where the relevant business object supports it. Situation Handling can bring the business situation to the responsible user. EWM can execute the physical warehouse movement through its existing process. EWM execution history can provide the record of confirmed warehouse execution.

The capabilities work together, but they do not need to become one combined technical layer.

This is also why a notification should not automatically become an evidence repository, and an evidence repository should not automatically become the warehouse execution mechanism.

Direct Access: The Speed Layer

A user receiving a situation should not have to search through unrelated repositories simply to understand the exception.

The practical path should be as direct as the scenario allows:

Situation → Relevant Business Context → Evidence → Decision

Situation Handling provides the attention. GOS provides the evidence where supported by the relevant business object/application. EWM provides the physical execution.

The exact navigation or action available to the user depends on the Situation Handling scenario, business object, application and configuration.

In this article, I use "speed layer" as a design term for the shortest practical path from a business situation to its supporting evidence. It is not an SAP product name or a standard SAP architectural layer.

The principle is simple:

Do not create another technical layer merely to make information reachable when the existing business context can already provide the required path.

When the Business Says: "We Need History"

One of the easiest ways to overengineer an architecture is to say:

"We need history."

The next question should immediately be:

"History of what?"

If the business needs the photograph, it needs evidence. If it needs to know what warehouse movement occurred, it needs execution history. If it needs to know who was responsible for the situation, it needs situation and responsibility information. If it genuinely needs an enterprise document-management lifecycle, DMS may become relevant.

The word history by itself is not enough to determine the technical solution.

This becomes especially important for audit requirements.

An audit question may be: What did the operator see? What evidence was captured? Who performed the action? When did it happen? What warehouse movement was executed? Why was the decision taken?

These questions describe different types of information.

Therefore: audit requirement does not automatically mean DMS.

The better question is:

"What story does the audit need to reconstruct?"

If that story is already represented across the business situation, business object, supporting evidence and execution history, another repository may simply duplicate information rather than solve a new requirement.

DMS becomes relevant when the business genuinely requires structured document-management capabilities beyond what the existing business objects and processes provide.

When the Pattern Changes

This approach does not mean that GOS should always be used, Situation Handling should always be used, or DMS should never be used.

The requirement determines the capability.

A transportation exception may require TM capabilities. A maintenance-related requirement may require EAM capabilities. A warehouse execution requirement may require EWM capabilities. A genuine enterprise document-management requirement may require DMS.

The technical objects change according to the business context. The reasoning does not:

Business Requirement → Natural Capability → Configuration → Integration where required → Custom Development only where a real gap remains

That is the reusable part of the approach.

No Custom Code as the Foundation

Standard SAP capabilities should be considered before introducing custom development.

The fact that several SAP capabilities are involved does not automatically mean that a custom layer is required. Sometimes the cleaner architecture is simply to let each standard capability perform the responsibility it already owns.

Technical Implementation: Ground to SAP

The business-first design eventually has to reach the SAP implementation layer.

For evidence, the design can use GOS / Attachment, where supported by the relevant business object or application.

For business attention, Situation Handling can be used according to the applicable scenario and configuration. Manage Situation Types (F2947) is the relevant Fiori application for configuring situation types in supported scenarios.

For physical warehouse movement, the existing EWM process and warehouse tasks remain responsible for execution.

For confirmed warehouse execution history, /SCWM/ORDIM_C is the relevant EWM reference in this design.

The exact configuration path can depend on the SAP release and the specific Situation Handling or EWM scenario. Therefore, technical references should be validated against the actual release and application rather than treated as one universal configuration path.

The technical layer comes after the business requirement has been understood.

The Manyat Principle

The purpose of Manyat Thinking is not to reduce the number of SAP components.

It is to avoid making one component responsible for requirements that naturally belong to different capabilities.

The principle is:

Start with the business requirement, identify the SAP capability that naturally owns it, and avoid adding another layer unless the requirement genuinely needs it.

And one question keeps the architecture honest:

"Record of what?"

Core Manyat Pattern: Ground Reality → Exception → WHY → Business Requirement → SAP Capability → Technical Implementation → Business Action

Conclusion

A broken seal may look like a small warehouse exception, but it can expose a much larger architecture problem when every requirement is pushed into one technical mechanism.

The cleaner approach is to separate the requirements.

Let GOS / Attachment handle supporting evidence where appropriate. Let Situation Handling bring the relevant business situation to the responsible user. Let EWM handle the physical warehouse execution. Let EWM execution records provide the warehouse execution history. And let DMS handle genuine document-management requirements when they actually exist.

The objective is not to remove SAP capabilities. The objective is to make each capability responsible for the problem it naturally owns.

Start from the ground. Ask WHY. Identify the real requirement. Then let SAP capabilities do what they are designed to do.
